newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkish economy in need of structural reforms.
newsitem.headline: Turkish economy in need of structural reforms.

text.p: Turkey's economy will be in the doldrums this year and next year unless government-pledged structural reforms and a medium-term stability programme are immediately put in place, a prominent Turkish banker said.

"If structural measures are not advanced, economic balances not maintained through a medium-term stability programme and those efforts not backed by international institutions, the second half of 1997 and 1998 will be more difficult," said Unal Korukcu, general manager of the commercial Isbank .
He told reporters ahead of the bank's annual general meeting on Monday in Ankara that Turkey's economic woes could be tackled only by a firm stability programme.
"Officials say the stability programme will go into the agenda of the talks with international agencies like the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank," he said.

His remarks came one day ahead of the start of a two-week-long planned visit by an IMF team, who will hold talks with Turkey's economy officials and businessmen to seek ways to rescue the country's ailing economy.
"It is projected that the Turkish economy cannot sustain a growth based on demand rise and therefore should attach importance to measures that will boost stability," he said.
Turkey has announced a balanced budget for 1997 after a budget deficit of 1,217 trillion lira in 1996, or 8.2 percent of gross national product.
The budget deficit is mainly caused by loss-making state enterprises, most of which are slated for privatisation, farm subsidies and municipal spendings.

But Korukcu said: "It is predicted that without a medium-term stability programme, structural reforms and measures that will cut expenditures, public fiscal discipline cannot easily attain a healthy structure."
He urged the government to strictly apply a realistic exchange policy as well as take measures to boost exports to take the burden off the balance of payments.
The current account gave a $2.31 billion deficit in the first half of 1996 and officials have estimated it would reach $6 to $7 billion for the whole 1996, up from $2.3 billion a year ago.
Turkey's foreign trade deficit, a major hole for the current account deficits, is expected to rise to around $20 billion for 1996 from $14.1 billion in 1995.
Korukcu predicted the ratio of the public sector borrowing requirement (PSBR) to gross national product (GNP) will rise to 9.6 percent in 1996 from 5.4 percent a year ago.
The treasury's outstanding domestic debt rose to 3,149 trillion lira at end-1996 form 1,361 trillion a year ago, and foreign debt stands at about $78 billion.
Korukcu said Turkey's economic growth for 1997, targeted at four percent, could rise more than that because "current practices are not carried out in such a way to cut consumption."

Turkey announced on Monday that its GNP growth was 7.9 percent in 1996, up from eight percent in 1995, amid worries the figure could signal trouble for the country's already high debts and inflation, which runs about 78 percent annually. Gross domestic product grew by 7.2 percent in 1996.

Korukcu said he expected individual and corporate banking activities would increase in 1997 and urged Turkish banks to take care in the management of assets and liabilities in view of new government debt instruments and political uncertainties.
The treasury will auction on Tuesday two-year, inflation times risk premium bonds with three-month interest payments. The government issued a similar bond earlier this month for the first time.
